\begin{abstract}
\noindent
A backtest is one draw from a distribution of histories that never got run. Indian equity markets
since 2015 contain roughly one pandemic crash, one full rate cycle and one structural liquidity
shift, so a claim that a strategy is ``robust across regimes'' rests on a handful of effective
observations no matter how many sessions were simulated. \textbf{We release RegimeStress: a
benchmark, protocol and reference implementation for measuring how much a strategy's performance
moves when the market environment is varied, rather than how high it is on the environment that
happened.}

\paragraph{What the benchmark provides.} A causally-labelled regime series over
\rsNLabelledSessions\ sessions, estimated by expanding-window refits with a forward-only decode so
that no label uses information from after the session it describes; \textbf{Counterfactual Regime
Resampling (CRR)}, a stationary block bootstrap conditioned on regime label that generates
synthetic-but-plausible market histories; a moment-validation suite the synthetic paths must pass;
two stress tiers of very different cost; a frozen strategy population with its exclusion criteria
fixed \emph{before} any stress path was run; and a fully reproducible pipeline in which every
number in this paper is generated from the committed artifacts rather than transcribed.

\keyfinding{\textbf{The cheap stress tier reproduces performance well and fragility poorly.}
Resampling a strategy's \emph{realised} returns agrees with full counterfactual re-simulation at
Spearman \rsTierAgreementMeanSharpe\ on mean performance but only \rsTierAgreementFragility\ on
fragility (n\;=\;\rsTierAgreementN). The divergence is \emph{consistent with} strategy re-decision
contributing materially to measured fragility: the two tiers differ in whether a strategy may
respond to the path it is given, and it is fragility rather than performance that the cheap tier
loses. We do not claim causation from a rank correlation. We report the divergence as an empirical
methodological result with a practical consequence: the expensive tier is not optional.}

\paragraph{A shortcut that does hold.} Not every shortcut fails, and the benchmark distinguishes
them by measurement rather than by assertion. Across-regime fragility computed directly from a
strategy's persisted return series agrees with its bootstrapped counterpart at Spearman
\rsShortcutSpearman\ (n\;=\;\rsShortcutN). The expensive \rsTierOneCpuHours-CPU-hour experiment
was run in full and then used to \emph{validate} the free computation rather than being replaced
by an assumption about it.

\paragraph{Fragility prediction: a null, and its diagnosis.} Whether fragility can be predicted
from strategy characteristics alone --- turnover, holding period, concentration, factor exposures
--- is the benchmark's first task. It cannot, at this sample size. Across
\rsPredictorRows\ strategies and \rsPredictorFeatures\ features, five models on identical folds
reach an out-of-sample $R^2$ of \rsPathsRawBestRsquared\ on the primary target. A permutation test
over \rsPermutations\ shuffles nonetheless rejects the null for the \emph{ranking}
(p\;=\;\rsRegimesLogPermPSpearman--\rsPathsRawPermPSpearman) while failing to reject it for the
\emph{level} on three of four targets. \textbf{Strategy characteristics contain statistically
detectable ranking information and very weak information about the absolute level of fragility.}
We show the limitation is data variance rather than model bias --- every model fits its training
folds far better than it generalises, and the gap is \emph{widest} for the model with the most
capacity --- and therefore add no capacity.

\paragraph{Two corrections, reported as findings.} Our own first result was better and wrong.
Deduplicating the corpus revealed \rsDuplicateClusters\ clusters of strategies with identical
realised return series; a duplicate in a training fold with its twin in the test fold was worth
\rsLeakageDelta\ of $R^2$. A second defect had one feature column duplicating another under a
different name. Both are in the benchmark's corrections log, and the duplicate structure ships as
a benchmark artifact --- it is a fact about generated strategy corpora, not a blemish on ours.

\paragraph{Disposition.} RegimeStress is released as infrastructure to extend, not as a solved
problem. The environment, the resampler, the protocol and the exclusion rules are independent of
whether our fragility predictor worked, and a larger or more diverse corpus can be scored against
exactly the same apparatus.
\end{abstract}

\vspace{0.4em}

% -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Contributions}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em]
\item \textbf{The RegimeStress benchmark.} A frozen environment, strategy population, exclusion
protocol and evaluation harness for measuring strategy fragility, with every artifact regenerable
by a documented command sequence.

\item \textbf{Counterfactual Regime Resampling.} A stationary block bootstrap conditioned on
regime label, with block length selected by a stated automatic rule, generating synthetic market
histories that preserve cross-sectional structure because dates are resampled rather than assets.

\item \textbf{Causal regime labelling.} An expanding-window hidden Markov model with a forward-only
decode. We report what causality costs: \rsRegimeTerminalDisagreement\% of labels disagree with
what the same estimator says at the end of the sample, and we treat that drift as a property to be
reported rather than a defect to be smoothed away.

\item \textbf{Validation of the synthetic histories.} \rsNMoments\ target moments, compared against
the real series' position in the synthetic distribution. The conditional resampler fails
\rsMomentsFailedConditional; the unconditional one fails \rsMomentsFailedUnconditional. We report
the failure rather than modifying the resampler until it passes.

\item \textbf{An empirical result on when computational shortcuts are safe.} One shortcut is
validated at \rsShortcutSpearman\ and adopted; another is measured at \rsTierAgreementFragility\
and rejected. The benchmark's position is that this is an experiment, not a design decision.

\item \textbf{A diagnosed null result on fragility prediction}, separating heavy tails,
multicollinearity, influential observations, sample size and genuine weakness of relationship,
with the bias-versus-variance question settled by measurement.
\end{enumerate}

% =====================================================================================
\section{Why fragility needs a benchmark}

The question a portfolio manager asks after ``is this signal real?'' is ``when does it stop
working?'' The standard apparatus answers the first question much better than the second.
Cross-validation with purging and embargo \citep{lopezdeprado2018}, deflated performance statistics
\citep{bailey2014}, and multiple-testing corrections \citep{harvey2016} all address selection over
\emph{strategies}. None addresses selection over \emph{histories}. A strategy evaluated on
2020--2024 Indian equities has been tested against one sequence of events, and no amount of
statistical correction applied within that sequence tells you what would have happened had the
sequence been different.

Regime-switching models are the usual response \citep{hamilton1989, ang2012}: label the market
into states, evaluate within each. This helps, and it introduces two problems that are rarely
reported. The first is that regime labels are themselves \emph{fitted}, and fitting them on the
full sample before evaluating strategies inside them is a lookahead bias structurally identical to
the ones a careful backtest is built to prevent. The second is that the number of independent
regime observations is small --- far smaller than the number of sessions --- so per-regime
performance estimates are noisy in a way that per-session counts conceal.

RegimeStress addresses both, and makes the addressing measurable. Our position is that a benchmark
in this area is more useful than another method, for the same reason that shared benchmarks proved
more durable than individual systems in language understanding \citep{wang2019} and code generation
\citep{chen2021}: the apparatus outlives whichever model was state of the art when it was built.

\subsection{What this paper is not}

It is not a demonstration that fragility can be predicted. Our fragility predictor produces a null
result, reported in \S\ref{sec:prediction} with its diagnosis. It is not a claim that our synthetic
histories are the true distribution of counterfactual markets --- \S\ref{sec:threats} says at
length why they are not. And it is not a strategy paper: no strategy in the corpus is recommended,
and many of them lose money.

% =====================================================================================
\section{The benchmark}

\subsection{Population, and exclusions frozen in advance}

The input population is two groups kept distinguishable at every stage: strategies generated by a
local language model and audited in prior work, and a panel of standard academic factor strategies
that acts as a positive control. Pooling them would hide whichever effect is real.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Filter} & \thead{Count} \\
\midrule
Strategies entering calibration & \rsNCalibrated \\
Failed to execute at all & \rsNRuntimeFailures \\
Excluded: not deterministic functions of their inputs & \rsNNondeterministic \\
\quad of which standard academic factors & \rsNNondeterministicFactors \\
\midrule
Stressed & \rsNStressed \\
Excluded: knife-edge (\S\ref{sec:knifeedge}) & \rsNKnifeEdge \\
Excluded: exact duplicates (\S\ref{sec:duplicates}) & \rsDuplicateRemoved \\
\midrule
\textbf{In the fragility-prediction training set} & \textbf{\rsPredictorRows} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Nondeterminism.} \rsNNondeterministic\ strategies return a different result when run
twice on the same data with the same code, with a worst-case Sharpe swing of
\rsWorstNondeterministicSwing. Every one is generator output; every standard factor is
deterministic. The census was frozen before any stress path was run, which matters: a determinism
filter chosen after seeing stress results is a selection rule masquerading as hygiene.

\subsection{Causal regime labelling}

Regimes come from a Gaussian hidden Markov model \citep{rabiner1989} on realised-volatility
features. Three properties are enforced structurally rather than by convention.

\textbf{The state count is selected once and frozen.} $K = \rsRegimeK$, chosen by BIC
\citep{schwarz1978} on \rsRegimeSelectionSessions\ sessions ending \rsRegimeSelectionEnd, entirely
before the evaluation window. Later refits re-estimate parameters and may never re-select $K$; the
selection artifact is write-once and the script exits with an error if run again.

\textbf{Parameters are re-estimated on an expanding window}, at each quarterly rebalance date, on
sessions strictly prior to it. The first refit sees \rsRegimeTrainingSessionsFirst\ sessions and
the last \rsRegimeTrainingSessionsLast.

\textbf{The decode is forward-only.} This is the part most easily got wrong. Standard HMM libraries
offer Viterbi decoding and smoothed posteriors, and \emph{both} decide the state at session $t$
using observations after $t$. Neither is admissible here. Labels come from
$\arg\max_k P(\text{state}_t \mid \text{obs}_{1:t})$ --- what an observer standing at $t$ could
have known. The cost is a lag of about two sessions at turning points.

\begin{selfreport}[title={What causality costs, reported rather than hidden}]
\rsRegimeTerminalDisagreement\% of labels disagree with what the same estimator assigns at the end
of the sample, and \rsRegimeRevisionRate\% are revised within one quarter. The disagreement is
strongly concentrated: calm later years entered the expanding window and recalibrated what
``normal'' volatility means, so earlier sessions read as more elevated in hindsight.

\textbf{Consequence, binding on every result in this paper:} ``state 2 in 2022'' and ``state 2 in
2024'' are not the same conditioning event. Per-period summaries are primary; pooled summaries
carry this note. A full-sample fit would have made the labels stable and the analysis invalid.
\end{selfreport}

The regime series is independently anchored: the index closes it is fitted on were compared against
the exchange's own published index files on \rsBurninCompared\ sessions, with
\rsBurninBeyondTolerance\ beyond tolerance and a worst relative difference of
$\rsBurninWorstRelative$. The benchmark also ships a hand-curated timeline of \rsNSebiEvents\ dated
market-structure events, each carrying an evidence grade so a reader can see which entries rest on
a regulatory circular and which on secondary reporting.

\subsection{Counterfactual Regime Resampling}

CRR generates synthetic market histories by stationary block bootstrap
\citep{politis1994}, with block length selected by the automatic rule of \citet{politis2004} as
corrected by \citet{patton2009}: $\rsBlockLength$ sessions at a bandwidth of \rsBlockBandwidth.
Two design choices carry the method.

\textbf{Dates are resampled, not assets.} A block is a contiguous run of \emph{sessions}, carried
across the whole cross-section at once. This preserves the correlation structure between stocks
exactly, at the cost of preserving it \emph{too} exactly --- see \S\ref{sec:threats}.

\textbf{Blocks are drawn conditional on regime label}, so a synthetic history is assembled from
blocks that resemble the regime they are placed into. This is what makes the moments pass.

\subsection{Validating the synthetic histories}

A resampler that produces implausible histories produces meaningless stress results, so the
benchmark requires the synthetic paths to reproduce the real series' distributional properties
before any strategy is run on them. \rsNMoments\ statistics are compared --- mean, dispersion,
skew, tail behaviour, and volatility clustering at several horizons --- by asking where the real
value falls in the distribution of \rsCrrPaths\ synthetic values over
\rsCrrWindowStart--\rsCrrWindowEnd.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Resampler} & \thead{Moments tested} & \thead{Outside the 95\% interval} \\
\midrule
Conditional on regime & \rsNMoments & \rsMomentsFailedConditional \\
Unconditional & \rsNMoments & \rsMomentsFailedUnconditional \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The unconditional resampler fails a single long-horizon volatility-clustering statistic, with the
real value at the \rsFailingMomentPercentile th percentile of the synthetic distribution.

\begin{finding}
\textbf{The failure is reported, not repaired.} We did not adjust the resampler until the statistic
passed. Conditional resampling is primary and unconditional is retained as an ablation, so the
difference between them is an experimental result rather than an assertion about which is better.
Conditioning turns out to be nearly free in ranking terms --- across-path fragility ranks agree at
Spearman \rsConditioningEffectPaths\ between the two --- but it is what makes the moments pass.
\end{finding}

\subsection{Two tiers, and two definitions of fragility}

Fragility is the ratio of the variance of performance across environments to its mean:
\[
  F(s) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{e}\!\left[\pi(s, e)\right]}
                  {\mathbb{E}_{e}\!\left[\pi(s, e)\right]}.
\]
The benchmark computes it two ways, because $e$ can range over two different things. \textbf{Across
regimes}, $e$ indexes the regime labels within the one real history. \textbf{Across paths}, $e$
indexes synthetic histories. These are not interchangeable: they agree at Spearman
\rsDefinitionAgreement\ (n\;=\;\rsTierAgreementN), and both are reported.

The two \emph{tiers} are two ways of obtaining $\pi(s, e)$ on a synthetic path:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Tier 1 (faithful).} Rebuild the entire price panel from resampled blocks, then re-run
every strategy on it. Strategies re-decide: a momentum strategy on a synthetic path buys whatever
that path made a winner. Cost: \rsTierOneCpuHours\ CPU-hours for \rsTierOnePaths\ paths, a median
of \rsTierOneSecondsPerPath\ seconds per path.
\item \textbf{Tier 2 (cheap).} Bootstrap each strategy's \emph{realised} return series directly.
The strategy's decisions are fixed; only their order is varied. Cost: \rsTierTwoSeconds\ seconds
for \rsTierTwoPaths\ paths.
\end{itemize}

The ratio in cost is roughly four orders of magnitude, which is exactly why the comparison in
\S\ref{sec:tiers} is worth making.

\subsection{Reproducibility, and how every number here was produced}

Seed 42 throughout; every stochastic operation takes an explicit seed. Every script writes a run
manifest recording git SHA, package versions, input hashes, model tags and wall-clock duration.
All inference is local.

\textbf{No figure in this paper was typed by hand.} A generator reads the frozen artifacts and
emits every quantitative claim as a LaTeX macro, with the artifact each value came from recorded
alongside it; the paper body contains macros only. This is deliberately stricter than our earlier
work, where numbers were transcribed from committed reports --- correct in practice, but a
transcription error would have been indistinguishable from a result.

\textbf{The guarantee is enforced rather than asserted, and the enforcement was itself tested.} A
checker strips structural \LaTeX{} from the body and fails the build if any numeric literal
survives outside a short allowlist of protocol constants --- seeds, exponents, years, the nominal
confidence level --- each of which carries a written reason for not being a measurement. Because a
gate nobody has seen fail is indistinguishable from a gate that cannot fail, we ran the negative
control: a figure was typed into a claim sentence in place of its macro, and the checker rejected
the paper and named the offending line. It was then reverted. That control now runs on the real
paper source as part of the test suite, in both directions --- the committed paper must pass, and a
tampered copy of it must fail --- so the guarantee cannot quietly lapse.

% =====================================================================================
\section{Results}

\subsection{Tier 2 reproduces performance, not fragility}\label{sec:tiers}

The central methodological experiment: does the cheap tier substitute for the expensive one?

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Quantity} & \thead{Spearman, Tier 1 vs Tier 2} & \thead{n} \\
\midrule
Mean performance & \rsTierAgreementMeanSharpe & \rsTierAgreementN \\
\textbf{Fragility} & \textbf{\rsTierAgreementFragility} & \rsTierAgreementN \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{finding}
\textbf{The answer is no, and the shape of the failure is informative.} Tier 2 ranks strategies by
performance almost as well as full re-simulation (\rsTierAgreementMeanSharpe) and ranks them by
fragility considerably worse (\rsTierAgreementFragility). Median fragility differs as well:
\rsTierMedianOne\ under Tier 1 against \rsTierMedianTwo\ under Tier 2.

The two tiers differ in exactly one respect: Tier 2 varies the \emph{order} of outcomes a strategy
already produced, while Tier 1 varies the \emph{world} and lets the strategy respond to it. That a
shortcut preserving decisions loses most of the fragility signal while preserving most of the
performance signal is \emph{consistent with} strategy re-decision contributing materially to
measured fragility.

\textbf{We stop short of claiming that as a cause.} Two rank correlations computed on one corpus
cannot establish a mechanism, and at least one alternative explanation survives: fragility is a
variance-like quantity and therefore a noisier statistic than mean performance, so a lower
correlation is partly expected on estimation grounds alone. Separating the two would require an
experiment we did not run --- for instance a Tier 1 variant in which the panel is resampled but
each strategy's positions are frozen to its real-history book. We name it here as the obvious next
measurement rather than assert the conclusion it would test.

What does not depend on the interpretation is the practical consequence: whatever produces the
gap, Tier 2 cannot be substituted for Tier 1 when fragility is the quantity of interest.
\end{finding}

We expected Tier 2 to be an adequate approximation and built it as the default. It is not, and the
benchmark reports it as an entry rather than removing the tier. Tier 2 remains useful for the
question it does answer well, and it is retained so that future work can measure how the gap
behaves on a different corpus.

\subsection{A shortcut that does hold}

Across-regime fragility can be computed directly from a strategy's persisted return series at no
simulation cost. The question is whether the free computation preserves the ranking the expensive
one produces.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Quantity} & \thead{Value} \\
\midrule
Spearman, direct computation vs bootstrap (n\;=\;\rsShortcutN) & \textbf{\rsShortcutSpearman} \\
Median fragility, direct & \rsShortcutMedianReal \\
Median fragility, bootstrap & \rsShortcutMedianBootstrap \\
Rank convergence at \rsConvergenceLowPaths\ paths & \rsConvergenceLow \\
Rank convergence at \rsConvergenceHighPaths\ paths & \rsConvergenceHigh \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{finding}
\textbf{The expensive Tier 1 stress experiment served two purposes: (1) measuring across-path
fragility under genuine strategy re-optimisation on synthetic market histories, and (2) empirically
validating that the inexpensive computation of across-regime fragility from persisted real return
series produces essentially the same ranking (Spearman $\approx$ \rsShortcutSpearman), eliminating
the need for an otherwise redundant rerun.}
\end{finding}

The ordering matters. The costly experiment was run first, in full, and then used to establish that
a rerun would reproduce a ranking already available for free. It was not skipped and justified
afterwards. Taken together with \S\ref{sec:tiers}, the benchmark's position on computational
shortcuts is that whether one is safe is an empirical question with a measurable answer, and that
the answer differs between shortcuts that look equally reasonable beforehand.

\subsection{Three properties of the population, reported as findings}\label{sec:knifeedge}

The next three results are facts about the strategies and about the fragility metric itself. They
also appear in Threats to Validity, because each limits what the rest of the paper can claim. They
are stated here as well because a reader who meets them only among the caveats would reasonably
conclude we had tried to keep them quiet.

\subsubsection*{A large minority of machine-generated strategies are not deterministic}

\rsNNondeterministic\ of \rsNCalibrated\ strategies return a different result when run twice on the
same data with the same code, with a worst-case Sharpe swing of \rsWorstNondeterministicSwing.

\begin{finding}
\textbf{Every affected strategy is generator output. Every standard academic factor is
deterministic.} This is a property of what the model wrote, not of the engine or the harness, and
it has a direct consequence for the whole enterprise: a strategy whose score already varies for no
reason is arithmetically indistinguishable from one whose score varies because the market changed.
Nondeterminism and fragility are the same measurement until the first is excluded.

We report the exclusion as a non-random one. The benchmark measures fragility on the subset of
machine-generated strategies that happen to be reproducible, and reproducibility may correlate with
the simplicity that also drives fragility. The census was frozen before any stress path was run.
\end{finding}

\subsubsection*{The stability filter removes the fast end of the corpus}

A strategy is \emph{knife-edge} if its Sharpe ratio is not stable under a numerically negligible
change to its inputs --- a relative perturbation on the order of $10^{-15}$, which no economic
interpretation survives. \rsKnifeEdgeExcluded\ of \rsNStressed\ qualify, including
\rsKnifeEdgeFactors\ standard academic factor. The rule was applied without exemption.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Median characteristic} & \thead{Excluded} & \thead{Retained} \\
\midrule
Count & \rsKnifeEdgeExcluded & \rsKnifeEdgeRetained \\
Turnover per session & \rsKnifeEdgeTurnoverExcluded & \rsKnifeEdgeTurnoverRetained \\
Holding period (sessions) & \rsKnifeEdgeHoldingExcluded & \rsKnifeEdgeHoldingRetained \\
Effective holdings & \rsKnifeEdgeHoldingsExcluded & \rsKnifeEdgeHoldingsRetained \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{selfreport}[title={The exclusion is not random, and that is a limitation of our results}]
The excluded strategies are systematically the \emph{fast} end of the corpus: twenty times the
turnover and a twentieth of the holding period of those retained. Every result downstream is
therefore conditioned on a restricted range of exactly the characteristic most likely to drive
fragility. Sharpe swing among the excluded has a median of \rsKnifeEdgeSwingMedian\ and a maximum
of \rsKnifeEdgeSwingMax, with \rsKnifeEdgeSwingAboveHalf\ above 0.5 --- so for most of them the
instability is small, and for a few it is not.
\end{selfreport}

\subsubsection*{A strategy that is uniformly bad is measured as stable}

Fragility is a ratio with a mean in its denominator, and it scores \emph{consistency}, not quality.
Nothing prevents a strategy that loses money in every regime from being uniformly consistent about
it.

\begin{finding}
\textbf{This is not hypothetical, and it is not rare.} \rsUniformlyBadCount\ of \rsNPrimary\
strategies have a negative Sharpe ratio in \emph{every} labelled regime. The most extreme,
\texttt{\rsUniformlyBadName}, ranges from \rsUniformlyBadWorstSharpe\ to
\rsUniformlyBadBestSharpe\ across the four regimes --- and with a fragility of
\rsUniformlyBadFragility\ it ranks \rsUniformlyBadRank\ of \rsNPrimary\ on the low-fragility end of
the corpus. It is among the most robust strategies we measured, and it never makes money.

\textbf{A fragility score is therefore uninterpretable without a performance figure beside it}, and
must never be used as a standalone ranking. Our narrative layer does not enforce this and describes
one such strategy as most reliable in a regime in which it loses money. A further \rsNNearZeroMean\
strategies are flagged because a near-zero mean in the denominator inflates the ratio for
arithmetic reasons; how many sit close enough to that boundary for the flag to miss them is
unknown.
\end{finding}

\subsection{Fragility prediction, and its diagnosis}\label{sec:prediction}

The benchmark's first task: predict a strategy's fragility from its characteristics alone ---
turnover, holding period, concentration, book-similarity decay, and factor exposures obtained from
one joint regression on all factors at once --- without running the stress suite.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Model} & \thead{$R^2$} & \thead{train $R^2$} & \thead{gap} & \thead{$\rho$} &
\thead{MAE} & \thead{$R^2$ drop-5} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{7}{@{}l}{\emph{Primary target: fragility across synthetic paths, raw}
  \hfill baseline MAE \rsPathsRawBaselineMae} \\
Ridge & \rsPathsRawRidgeRsquared & \rsPathsRawRidgeTrainRsquared & \rsPathsRawRidgeGap &
  \rsPathsRawRidgeSpearman & \rsPathsRawRidgeMae & \rsPathsRawRidgeDropFive \\

  \rsRegimesLogLassoSpearman & \rsRegimesLogLassoMae & \rsRegimesLogLassoDropFive \\
Elastic net & \rsRegimesLogElasticNetRsquared & \rsRegimesLogElasticNetTrainRsquared &

\textbf{Random forest} & \textbf{\rsRegimesLogForestRsquared} &
  \rsRegimesLogForestTrainRsquared & \rsRegimesLogForestGap & \rsRegimesLogForestSpearman &
  \textbf{\rsRegimesLogForestMae} & \textbf{\rsRegimesLogForestDropFive} \\

\caption{Five models, identical folds, identical seed, n\;=\;\rsPredictorRows. \emph{gap} is train
$R^2$ minus out-of-fold $R^2$. \emph{drop-5} recomputes $R^2$ after removing the five largest

\end{table}

\paragraph{Is there any signal at all?} A permutation test over \rsPermutations\ shuffles separates
this from the question of how well it is fit. The observed rank correlation exceeds the null's 95th
percentile on all four target specifications, at
p\;=\;\rsRegimesLogPermPSpearman--\rsPathsRawPermPSpearman. The observed $R^2$ does not:
p\;=\;\rsPathsRawPermPRsquared, \rsPathsLogPermPRsquared\ and \rsRegimesRawPermPRsquared\ on three
targets, reaching significance only on the fourth (\rsRegimesLogPermPRsquared).

\begin{finding}
\textbf{Strategy characteristics contain statistically detectable information about the fragility
\emph{ranking}, and very weak information about its \emph{level}.} That is the benchmark's first
reported result, and it is a null with respect to the useful version of the question.
\end{finding}

\paragraph{Why, in five parts.} A null is only worth publishing if it is diagnosed, so we separated
the candidate causes rather than stopping at ``the model does not work''.

\begin{table}[h]\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.55\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\thead{Cause} & \thead{Verdict} & \thead{Evidence} \\
\midrule
Heavy-tailed target & \textbf{Dominant} &
  The five largest of \rsPredictorRows\ rows own \rsPathsRawTailShareFive\% of the total sum of
  squares (skew \rsPathsRawSkew, excess kurtosis \rsPathsRawKurtosis). An $R^2$ on this target is
  arithmetically a statement about five strategies. A log transform reduces the share to
  \rsPathsLogTailShareFive\%. \\
Multicollinearity & \textbf{Secondary} &
  Condition number \rsFeatureCondition; \texttt{\rsFeatureWorstPairA} and
  \texttt{\rsFeatureWorstPairB} correlate at $|r| = \rsFeatureWorstPairR$. It destabilises the
  linear models severely and leaves the trees alone, so it is not what limits the ranking. \\
Influential observations & \textbf{Confirmed} &
  Removing one strategy (\texttt{\rsPathsRawInfluenceWorst}) moves out-of-fold $R^2$ by
  \rsPathsRawInfluenceLargest, at fixed fold assignment. \\
Insufficient sample & \textbf{Contributor} &
  The learning curve is still climbing at the largest size available:
  $\rho$ \rsPathsLogCurveAtForty\ at n\;=\;\rsCurveSizeAtForty\ rising to
  \rsPathsLogCurveAtHundred\ at n\;=\;\rsCurveSizeAtHundred. It has not saturated. \\
Genuinely weak relationship & \textbf{Partly rejected} &
  Permutation test as above: real rank information, essentially no level information. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Bias or variance?} This decides whether a larger model is warranted, so it was settled
by measurement before any was considered. Every model fits its training folds better than it
generalises, and the gap is \emph{widest} for the highest-capacity model: gradient boosting reaches
\rsRegimesLogBoostingTrainRsquared\ in sample against \rsRegimesLogBoostingRsquared\ out of it, a
gap of \rsRegimesLogBoostingGap, while the conservative random forest --- the lowest-capacity tree
model --- attains both the best out-of-fold $R^2$ (\rsRegimesLogForestRsquared) and by far the best
trimming stability (\rsRegimesLogForestDropFive\ at drop-5 against
\rsRegimesLogBoostingDropFive).

\begin{finding}
\textbf{Nothing underfits.} The limitation is data variance, not model bias. We therefore added no
capacity: no larger ensemble, no gradient-boosting tuning, no neural network. The binding
constraints are \rsPredictorRows\ rows, a target whose variance sits in five of them, and one
shared market history.
\end{finding}

\paragraph{Which characteristics matter.} After deduplication and the switch to joint factor
regression, the leading permutation importances are
\texttt{\rsImportanceFirstName} (\rsImportanceFirstValue),
\texttt{\rsImportanceSecondName} (\rsImportanceSecondValue),
\texttt{\rsImportanceThirdName} (\rsImportanceThirdValue) and
\texttt{\rsImportanceFourthName} (\rsImportanceFourthValue). Structural characteristics --- how
often a strategy trades, how long it holds --- displaced the factor-exposure fingerprints that led
the earlier, contaminated ranking. Given the weakness of the underlying relationship, we present
this ordering as descriptive and do not build an argument on it.

\subsection{Two corrections, and why they are in the results}\label{sec:duplicates}

Our first predictor result was better than the one above and was wrong. We report the sequence
because the correction is more informative than either number.

\begin{selfreport}[title={C1 --- duplicate leakage}]
The generated corpus contains \rsDuplicateClusters\ clusters of strategies whose realised net
return series are \emph{identical} on every session, to within $10^{-12}$: different source code,
different stated rationale, same behaviour. \rsDuplicateMembers\ strategies sit in a cluster, the
largest containing \rsLargestDuplicateCluster; \rsDuplicateRemoved\ were removed.

Cross-validation assumes exchangeable rows. A duplicate sat in a training fold while its twin was
scored in the test fold. Same features, same folds, same seed, differing only in whether duplicates
are present: $R^2$ \rsLeakageWithDuplicates\ at n\;=\;\rsLeakageNWith\ against
\rsLeakageWithoutDuplicates\ at n\;=\;\rsLeakageNWithout. \textbf{The leakage was worth
\rsLeakageDelta\ of $R^2$}, and it was the difference between a positive headline and a null.

\rsNearDuplicatePairs\ further pairs correlating above \rsNearDuplicateThreshold\ were detected and
deliberately \emph{not} removed: any threshold chosen after seeing its effect on the result is the
pathology this programme exists to detect.
\end{selfreport}

\begin{selfreport}[title={C2 --- a feature column that was another feature column}]
One feature was another under a different name, correlating at exactly 1.000 and driving the design
matrix's condition number to the order of $10^{15}$ --- a numerically singular design handed to a
ridge regression as though it were well posed. Found by a collinearity diagnostic on its first
smoke run, not by a test.

Together, C1 and C2 also invalidated the feature importances we had previously reported: the top
feature vanished entirely and every magnitude fell by roughly a factor of three.
\end{selfreport}

Duplicate structure ships with the benchmark as an artifact rather than being cleaned away. It is a
property of language-model strategy corpora --- one candidate in the corpus turned out to be
identical in realised returns to the equal-weight baseline it was supposed to beat --- and a future
generator can be scored on how much of its output is redundant.

\subsection{Stress narratives}

A local model (\texttt{\rsNarrativeModel}, temperature 0, seed 42) generates natural-language
explanations of the most and least fragile strategies, from a prompt containing only measured
facts, which are stored alongside each narrative so any claim can be audited.

\begin{selfreport}[title={The weakest component, presented as illustrative}]
\rsNarrativeCount\ narratives were generated at \rsNarrativeSeconds\ seconds each. They are
factually correct and near-vacuous: they restate the fragility measurement rather than explain it,
and none used the turnover, holding-period or concentration facts supplied to them. One describes a
strategy as most reliable in a regime in which it loses money --- correct on the measurement, since
fragility scores consistency rather than quality, and unhelpful to a reader.

We report this rather than iterating on prompts until the output reads better, which would tune an
explainability layer against our own impression of it.
\end{selfreport}

% =====================================================================================
\section{Threats to validity}\label{sec:threats}

These are the reasons a reader should discount what is above. They are a section rather than a
footnote because several of them are load-bearing.

\paragraph{T1 --- The synthetic histories are an assumption, not evidence.} Across-path fragility
rests on \rsTierOnePaths\ counterfactual panels that never happened. The resampler reproduces
\rsNMoments\ of \rsNMoments\ target moments under conditional resampling, but reproducing marginal
moments is a far weaker claim than reproducing the data-generating process. Every conclusion
resting on across-path fragility inherits this in full.

\paragraph{T2 --- Conditional resampling does not preserve regime transitions.} A bootstrap jump
never changes label, so a synthetic path can dwell in one regime far longer than history ever did.
Regime persistence in the synthetic data is an artefact of the block length
($\rsBlockLength$ sessions), not of the market. The distortion is documented and unmeasured.

\paragraph{T3 --- The regime labels are fitted, and the resampler conditions on them.} Labels come
from an HMM fitted on the same price series the strategies trade, and CRR conditions on those
labels. The circularity is real and we have not quantified it. Separately, the expanding-window
design means label definitions drift over the sample
(\rsRegimeTerminalDisagreement\% terminal disagreement), so a ``regime'' is not a fixed
conditioning event.

\paragraph{T4 --- Excluding nondeterministic strategies removes a non-random group.}
\textbf{Reported as a finding in \S\ref{sec:knifeedge}; repeated here as a limitation.} All
\rsNNondeterministic\ excluded strategies are generator output and none are standard factors. The
benchmark therefore measures fragility on the subset of machine-generated strategies that happen to
be reproducible, and reproducibility may correlate with the simplicity that also drives fragility.

\paragraph{T5 --- Excluding knife-edge strategies removes the fast end of the corpus.}
\textbf{Reported as a finding in \S\ref{sec:knifeedge}; repeated here as a limitation.} The
\rsKnifeEdgeExcluded\ excluded strategies have roughly twenty times the turnover and a twentieth of
the holding period of those retained, so the predictor is trained on a restricted range of the
characteristic most likely to matter.

\paragraph{T6 --- Tier 2 does not measure what it was built to measure.} It is retained in the
benchmark and reported honestly, but any future use of it as a fragility proxy is unsupported by
our own evidence (\S\ref{sec:tiers}).

\paragraph{T7 --- The predictor's sample is small, and its rows are not independent.}
\rsPredictorRows\ strategies, summarised over the same market window. There is no time axis to
purge --- rows are strategies, not periods --- but the cross-validation still treats as independent
observations that share one realisation of the market. Every confidence interval here is narrower
than the truth. The learning curve has not saturated.

\paragraph{T8 --- Fragility is a ratio with a mean in its denominator, and it scores
consistency rather than quality.} \textbf{Reported as a finding in \S\ref{sec:knifeedge}; repeated
here as a limitation.} \rsUniformlyBadCount\ of \rsNPrimary\ strategies lose money in every regime
and are scored as among the least fragile in the corpus. Separately, strategies whose mean
performance is near zero carry a large fragility for an arithmetic rather than an economic reason;
\rsNNearZeroMean\ are flagged rather than dropped, and how many sit close enough to the boundary for
the flag to miss them is unknown. \textbf{A fragility score must never be read without a
performance figure beside it.}

\paragraph{T9 --- The signal-decay characteristic is a proxy.} The engine stores the book a
strategy produced, not the alpha forecast behind it, so book-similarity decay measures how fast the
realised portfolio turns over. A strategy with a fast signal and a slow rebalancing rule looks slow.

\paragraph{T10 --- External validity: one market, one asset class, one period, one generator.}
Every result is Indian equities, daily bars, a five-year window, and a corpus written largely by a
single 7B local model. Nothing here establishes that the tier comparison, the shortcut validation
or the prediction null would replicate on US equities, on intraday horizons, or on strategies
written by people.

% =====================================================================================
\section{Future research}

RegimeStress is released as infrastructure to extend rather than as a completed solution. The
following are open, and the benchmark is built so that each can be attempted without rebuilding the
apparatus.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Larger and more diverse strategy corpora.} The single strongest intervention our own
diagnosis supports. The learning curve suggests that larger strategy corpora may substantially
improve predictive performance; we leave this as future work. A corpus from several generators
would also separate ``fragility is hard to predict'' from ``fragility is hard to predict
\emph{for strategies this generator writes}''.

\item \textbf{Additional markets and asset classes.} The apparatus is not specific to India. A
market with a different participant mix would test whether the tier gap in \S\ref{sec:tiers} is a
property of stress testing or of this market's dynamics.

\item \textbf{Richer regime models.} Ours labels on volatility features alone. Liquidity, macro
state and market-structure epochs are all shipped with the benchmark and unused by the labeller.
Regime-switching models with duration dependence would also address T2 directly.

\item \textbf{Improved fragility predictors with larger datasets.} We deliberately did not add
model capacity, because the evidence pointed at variance. That conclusion is conditional on
\rsPredictorRows\ rows and should be revisited at ten times the sample.

\item \textbf{Alternative stress-generation methods.} Block bootstrap is one choice among several.
Generative models of price paths, regime-switching simulators with estimated transition matrices,
and historical-analogue methods would each fail differently, and CRR's moment suite is a ready
yardstick for comparing them.

\item \textbf{Extension to intraday strategies.} Daily bars bound what can be said about fast
strategies --- which is also, uncomfortably, the group our knife-edge filter removes.

\item \textbf{Evaluating future LLM strategy generators against RegimeStress.} The frozen
population, exclusion protocol and fragility definitions give a stable target. A stronger generator
can be scored on the same apparatus, including on the duplicate structure of its output, which our
corpus turned out to have in quantity.
\end{itemize}

% =====================================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

We set out to measure when trading strategies break, and the durable output is the measuring
apparatus rather than any strategy-level finding.

Three results are worth restating. Regime labelling can be done causally, and we report what it
costs rather than adopting the full-sample fit that would have made the labels look stable.
Computational shortcuts are an empirical question: one we tested was validated at Spearman
\rsShortcutSpearman\ and adopted, and another that looked equally reasonable reproduces fragility
at only \rsTierAgreementFragility\ and was rejected --- by the same experiment, run once, on the
same corpus. And fragility prediction from strategy characteristics yields a diagnosed null:
detectable ranking information, essentially no level information, limited by data variance rather
than model capacity.

Two of our own errors are in the results rather than in an appendix. Deduplicating the corpus
removed \rsLeakageDelta\ of $R^2$ that we had reported, and a duplicated feature column had made
the design matrix numerically singular. We think a benchmark that shows its corrections is more
useful than one that does not, and that the sequence --- optimistic result, robustness check,
falsification, diagnosis --- is the part of this work most worth reusing.

What we release is therefore an environment, a resampler with a validation suite, two stress tiers
with a measured account of when each is adequate, a frozen population with exclusion rules fixed in
advance, and a pipeline in which every number in this paper is generated from the artifacts rather
than transcribed. All of it is independent of whether our fragility predictor worked, which is
fortunate, because it did not.

\textbf{RegimeStress is intended as benchmark infrastructure rather than a completed scientific
result.} Future strategy generators, stress-generation methods and fragility predictors should be
evaluated against the same frozen protocol, so that progress is measured against a common standard
rather than against each new author's own apparatus. It is available at
\href{https://github.com/Ashwin-aadi/Trivijaya-Quant-Research}%
{\texttt{github.com/Ashwin-aadi/Trivijaya-Quant-Research}}.
